§ 2Content

§ 3Matter

  • Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. It can be solids, liquids, or gases. Matter is made up of tiny particles called atoms and molecules.

Based on the composition, matter can be classified as:

  1. 1. Pure Substances: Pure substances are substances that are made up of only one kind of particle and have a fixed or constant structure. E.g. Diamond, sulphur, tin, etc.
  2. 1. Element: A pure substance made up of only one type of atom that cannot be broken down into simpler substance by chemical means. E.g. H (Hydrogen) and O (Oxygen).
  3. 2. Compound: A pure substance made up of two or more different types of elements that are chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. E.g. H₂O (Water).
  4. 2. Impure Substances: Impure substances, also known as mixtures, are made up of two or more different substances. E.g. Brass (Cu+Zn), Bronze (Cu+Sn).

Four Fundamental States of Matter

Solids

  • They have distinct boundaries and fixed volumes.
  • They have a definite shape.
  • They have a tendency to maintain the shape when subjected to outside force.
  • Types of solids: Amorphous solids and Crystalline solids.
Amorphous SolidsCrystalline Solids
Isotropic in nature (same properties in all direction)Anisotropic in nature (properties vary with direction)
They have irregular shapeThey have a definite shape
They are pseudo solidsThey are true solids
They have an irregular arrangement of constituent particlesThey have a regular arrangement of constituent particles
They do not have sharp melting pointThey have sharp melting point
E.g. Glass, rubber, plastic, etc.E.g. Copper, Silver, NaCl

Liquid

  • A liquid is a state of matter that can flow and take the shape of its container.
Crystalline solid changes abruptly from solid to liquid when heated.

Gas

  • A gas is a substance that is in a gaseous, or vaporous, state of matter. It exhibits behaviour uniformity.

Plasma

  • It is the 4th state of matter.
  • A plasma is an ionised gas, with roughly equal numbers of positively and negatively charged particles.
  • It can be produced in laboratory by heating a gas to an extremely high temperature.
  • Stars are made of plasma.
States of MatterIntermolecular SpaceKinetic EnergyMovementForce of Attraction
SolidLowLowLowHigh
LiquidMediumMediumMediumMedium
GasHighHighHighLow

Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC)

  • The fifth state of matter is Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC).
  • It is typically formed when a gas of bosons at very low densities is cooled to temperatures very close to absolute zero, i.e., 0 K (−273.15°C; −459.67°F).
  • Origin of Name: The term "Boson" comes from the name of Dr. Satyendra Nath Bose, an Indian physicist whose work on quantum mechanics was extended by Albert Einstein in 1925.
  • Discovery: Dr. Bose published a research paper in 1924 and sent it to Einstein, who further developed the concept and predicted the existence of BEC in 1925.

First Production of Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC)

  • 1995: Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman experimentally produced the first BEC condensate in a rare field gas of rubidium atoms at extremely low temperature.
  • 1995: Wolfgang Ketterle later created a BEC condensate with sodium atoms. All three of them received Noble Prize in Physics in 2001.

Change in State of Matter

  • Sublimation: The process of changing a solid directly into a gas without passing through a liquid state. E.g. Naphthalene, dry ice, etc.
  • Deposition: The opposite of sublimation, where a gas turns into a solid without passing through a liquid state. E.g. The formation of frost or ice-crystals on surface.
  • Evaporation: The process of changing a liquid into a vapour by heating. This happens at boiling point of liquid. E.g. Evaporation of nail polish remover.
  • Condensation: The process by which water vapour in air changes into liquid. E.g. Dew, Fog.

Favourable Conditions for Evaporation

  • When temperature increases, the rate of evaporation increases.
  • When surface area increases, the rate of evaporation increases.
  • When wind speed increases, the rate of evaporation increases.
  • When humidity increases, the rate of evaporation decreases.

Mixture

  • A mixture is a composition of two or more pure substances. Mixtures are considered to be homogenous or heterogenous in nature.

Homogeneous Mixture vs Heterogeneous Mixture

Homogeneous MixtureHeterogeneous Mixture
They have a uniform compositionThey have a non-uniform composition
The components of mixture cannot be separated through physical processThe components can be separated through physical process
The component cannot be seen through naked eyesThe components can easily be seen through naked eyes
They exist in single-phaseThey can exist in two or more phase
E.g. A mixture of water and milkE.g. A mixture of oil in water

Solution

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture formed when one or more substances (solute) dissolve in another substance (solvent). The composition is uniform throughout, meaning the solute is evenly distributed within the solvent. E.g.
  • Liquid into liquid: Water and Ink.
  • Solid into Solid: Alloys.
  • Gas into Gas: Air.
  • Solid into a liquid: Sugar and Water.
  • Gas into Solid: Hydrogen dissolved in palladium.
  • Gas into Liquid: Carbon Dioxide dissolved in water.
1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m

Properties of Solution

  1. 1. It is homogeneous in nature.
  2. 2. The particles of solution are too small (less than 1 nm).
  3. 3. It does not scatter light.
  4. 4. It cannot be separated by filtration.
  5. 5. It is stable in nature.

More Examples of Solution

  • A solution of sugar in water is a solid in liquid solution. In this solution, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.
  • A solution of iodine in alcohol known as "Tincture of Iodine", this solution has iodine (solid) as the solute and alcohol (liquid) as the solvent. This solution is also used as Antiseptic.
  • Aerated drinks like soda water, etc., are gas in liquid solutions. These contain carbon dioxide (gas) as solute and water (liquid) as solvent.
  • Air is a mixture of gas in gas. Air is a homogeneous mixture of a number of gases. Its two main constituents are: oxygen (21%) and nitrogen (78%). The other gases are present in very small quantities.

Types of Solution

  1. 1. Unsaturated Solution: It is a solution that contains less solute than the maximum amount it can dissolve.
  2. 2. Saturated Solution: It is a solution that contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature.
  3. 3. Concentrated Solution: It contains a large amount of solute relative to the solvent.

Calculation of Mass % of a Solution

Mass % of solute = (Mass of Solute / Mass of Solution) × 100

Alloy

  • An alloy is a mixture of different metals or non metals that cannot be separated by physical method. E.g. Brass, Bronze, Nichrome, etc.

E.g. Q. A solution contains 40 g of common salt in 320 g of water. Calculate the concentration in terms of mass by mass % of the solution.

Solution: (40 / (40 + 320)) × 100 = 11.11% → Mass % of the solution

Suspension

...completely in the solvent, and its particles remain large enough to be seen with naked eye. E.g. Suspension may include muddy water, flour in water, and chalk powder in water.

Properties of Suspension

  • It is heterogeneous in nature.
  • It scatters light (shows Tyndall Effect) because particle size is large (greater than 1000 nm).
  • It can be separated using filtration method.
  • It is unstable because solute gets settled down in solvent.

Colloids

  • A colloid is a mixture in which one substance is dispersed evenly throughout another. Although colloids appear uniform (homogeneous) to the naked eye, they are actually heterogeneous when viewed under a microscope.
  • The particle size of colloid is intermediate (1-1000 nm) between that of a solution and suspension.

Examples of colloidal solution: Foam, Milk, Smoke, Detergents, Gel, Blood, Paint, Cosmetics.

Properties of Colloids

  • Colloids are heterogeneous in nature.
  • The particles cannot be seen through naked eyes (particle size: Between 1 and 1000 nm).
  • The particles of colloid do not settle down if left uninterrupted, hence they are stable.
  • It cannot be separated through filtration method but can be separated through centrifugation.
Turbidity measures the haziness or cloudiness of water due to suspended particles.

Tyndall Effect

  • When a beam of light is passed through a colloidal solution, the particles of the colloid scatters the beam of light and we can see the path of light in the solution. This is called as Tyndall Effect which was discovered in 1859.

Types of Colloids

Dispersed PhaseDispersing MediumTypeExample

Different Methods to Separate Components of a Mixture

  • We can separate the heterogeneous mixtures into their constituents by means of physical methods such as → Filtration, Hand-picking, Sieving.
  • Filtration: It is a physical separation process that separates solid matter and fluid from a mixture using a filter medium.
  • Hand-picking: It is a method of separating substances in a mixture by hand when the components are clearly visible enough to pick.
  • Sieving: It is a method of using a sieve to distinguish small particles from bigger particles.

Other Methods of Separation of components of Mixture

  1. 1. Evaporation: It is a process that is used to separate a mixture of a non-volatile and a volatile substance.

Applications (of Evaporation)

  • It is used to separate coloured dye from the ink.
  • It is used to separate salt from water.
  • It is used to separate sugar from water.
  1. 2. Chromatography: It is a technique used to separate different components of mixture that are soluble in same solvent.

Applications

  • It is used for separating different colors of a dye.
  • It is used to separate drugs from blood.
  1. 3. Centrifugation: It is a process that is used to separate dense particles from lighter particles.

Applications

  • It is used to separate cream from milk.
  • It is used to separate butter from cream.
  • It is used to squeeze out water from wet clothes.
  1. 4. Separating Funnel: It is a process that is used to separate two immiscible liquids.

Applications

  • It is used to separate oil from water.
  1. 5. Distillation: It is used to separate two miscible liquids (the boiling point of the liquids must be sufficiently different).

Application

  • It is used to separate acetone and water.

Types of Distillation

  1. 1. Simple Distillation: It is used to separate miscible liquids with boiling point differences of more than 25 Kelvin (or 25°C).
  2. 2. Fractional Distillation: It is used to separate miscible liquids with boiling point differences of less than 25 Kelvin (or 25°C). It is also used to separate components of air, like nitrogen and oxygen, based on their boiling points.
  1. 6. Sublimation: It is a process that is used to separate a sublimable component from non-sublimate component.

Application

  • It is used to separate ammonium chloride / camphor / naphthalene and salt.

Purifying Solids

Crystallisation

  • It is a process of formation of solid crystals from solution, melt, or by deposition directly from gas phase.
  • It is the most commonly used method for the process of purification of solids.
  • In this method, impure substances are dissolved in a minimum amount of water and then filtered.

Application

  • It is used to separate salt from seawater.
  • It is used for purification of copper sulphate.
Fractional Crystallization: It is the method of separating a mixture of soluble solids by dissolving them in a suitable hot solvent and then lowering the temperature slowly.

§ 4PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL CHANGES

Physical Properties of a Substance

  • The physical property of a substance is which we can observe, such as rigidity, colour, fluidity, boiling point, melting point, density, and hardness.

Chemical Properties of a Substance

  • The chemical nature of a substance is known as its chemical property, such as its order or its chemical composition.

Physical Change vs Chemical Change

Physical ChangeChemical Change
It is a change that occurs without changing the chemical composition of a matterIt is a change of chemical composition of a matter
It is usually reversibleIt is usually irreversible
New products are not formedNew products are formed
Some changes occur when heating or cooling it downChanges always involve absorption or release of energy
Changes have no effect on the chemical bonds of molecule of a substanceThey have a direct effect on the chemical bonds of molecules in a substance
  • Burning of candle is both physical and chemical change.
  • Thread: The thread undergoes chemical change, as it cannot be obtained again once burnt.
  • Wax: The wax undergoes physical change, as the wax can be used to make a new candle again.

Brownian Movement

  • It is a random zig-zag movement of particles suspended in a medium.
  • This motion is a result of the collisions of the particles with other fast-moving particles in the fluid.
  • It was named after Robert Brown after he discovered the phenomenon in 1827.

Types of Gases

Ideal GasReal Gas
The intermolecular force of attraction is zeroThere is some intermolecular force of attraction
It follows ideal gas equation → PV = nRT (P: Pressure; V: Volume; n: No. of moles; R = Universal gas constant; T = Temperature)
  • A real gas behaves most like an ideal gas at high temperatures and low pressures, where intermolecular forces and the volume occupied by the gas molecules become negligible.

Gas Laws

Boyle's Law (1662)

  • According to Boyle's Law, pressure and volume are inversely proportional to each other at constant temperature.
P ∝ 1/V ; P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
At constant T, as pressure increases, volume decreases

Charles' Law (1787)

  • According to Charles' Law, temperature and volume are directly proportional to each other at constant pressure.
V ∝ T ; V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂
At constant P, as temperature increases, volume increases.

Gay-Lussac's Law (1808)

  • According to Gay-Lussac's Law, pressure and temperature are directly proportional to each other at constant volume.
P ∝ T ; P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂
At constant V, as pressure increases, temperature increases.

Avogadro's Law (1811)

  • Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases under the same temperature and pressure conditions contain an equal number of molecules. In other words, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles of gas, when temperature and pressure are constant.
V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂
Solubility of gases in liquids increases with decrease in temperature.
